cues.text: Imagine you're going to have a stressful conversation.
Maybe you need to say something difficult.
Maybe you're worried about what the other person will say or think.
Or maybe you simply don't know how the conversation will go.
Before you have that conversation, take a few minutes for yourself.
Find a comfortable position and let your body relax.
You need this moment.
If you like, close your eyes.
For now, you don't need to plan what you're going to say.
You don't need to imagine what the other person might say.
Just take a slow breath in…
and breathe out.
Again, breathe in…
and slowly breathe out.
This conversation can wait for a few minutes.
Right now, you're here.
Just you and your breath.
Notice how your body feels when you think about this conversation.
Maybe your heart beats a little faster.
Maybe your hands start to move.
Maybe your body feels tense.
That's normal.
Sometimes, our body reacts to a difficult conversation before we even start talking.
Exhale slowly.
Now, think about what you need to say.
Maybe there's something important you need to bring up.
To bring up something means to start talking about a topic,
especially something you haven't talked about yet.
For example, maybe a friend did something that bothered you,
and you want to talk about it.
You could say, “There's something I want to bring up”,
which means “there's something I need to talk about.”
Take a slow breath in.
Think about what you might need to bring up in your conversation.
Imagine you're sitting across from the other person.
There's something you want to talk about, but you haven't said it yet.
When you're ready, you introduce the topic.
You bring it up.
Now it's something you can both talk about together.
Think, quietly, about how you'll bring the topic up.
Not the perfect words yet, just the feeling of it.
Steady.
Direct.
Calm, like someone setting something down gently, rather than dropping it suddenly,
or hiding it a moment longer.
Inhale.
Now, here's something equally important.
In most difficult conversations, there's also something you'll need to release,
something you won't be able to control once you've said your piece.
Maybe it's how the other person reacts.
Maybe it's needing them to fully understand you, immediately.
Maybe it's an old resentment you'd been holding onto, related to this same issue.
These are things you may need to drop.
Usually, to drop something means to let something fall from your hand.
But here,
to drop something means to stop talking about it or stop focusing on it because it isn't helping the situation anymore.
For example, if you keep arguing about the same thing, someone might say,
“Let's just drop it.” This means, “Let's stop talking about it and move on.”
Take a slow breath in.
Think about your conversation again.
What did you need to bring up?
Maybe there's something you need to say clearly.
Something you've been avoiding or waiting to talk about.
You don't need to find the perfect words right now.
Just notice what it is.
And breathe out.
Now ask yourself a different question: What can you drop?
Maybe you can drop the need to be right.
Maybe you can drop an argument that isn't going anywhere.
Maybe you can drop the need to control how the other person reacts.
You can choose what you bring up.
And you can choose what you drop.
Take another slow breath in.
Imagine yourself starting the conversation calmly.
You bring up what needs to be discussed.
You listen to what the other person has to say.
And if something isn't helping the conversation anymore, you allow yourself to drop it.
Breathe out slowly.
Remember, a difficult conversation doesn't have to be a perfect conversation.
You don't need to say everything perfectly.
You don't need to know exactly how the other person will respond.
You can only choose how you enter the conversation and how you communicate.
Take one final slow breath in.
And breathe out.
Before you open your eyes, remember these two ideas:
Bring up what needs to be said.
Drop what doesn't need to stay.
When you're ready, open your eyes.
Take your time.
And when the conversation begins, speak slowly, listen carefully, and remember:
you don't have to control every part of it.
You just have to take it one sentence at a time.
